qualifier: This page is for IP and trademark lawyers, in a firm or on their own, who want to move into tech law and work on the IP that tech companies are built on.
symptom_title: Searches, filings, oppositions, renewals. Then the next batch.
symptom: Your days are trademark searches, applications, examination replies, oppositions and renewal reminders. You are good at it, and much of it arrives in volume, with deadlines set by the registry rather than by you.

The clients who come to you often have a brand and little else to protect. When a software company does arrive, it wants a mark registered, while its bigger IP questions sit inside contracts someone else drafts.
You have probably wondered where your IP practice goes next. Copyright questions come in now and then, scattered across clients, and none of them add up to a field you can call your own.
outcome_title: IP work for the companies whose product is IP
outcome: Tech law means the legal work tech companies need, from contracts and compliance to privacy and disputes. For an IP lawyer it is a natural next field, because a software company's main asset is its code, its content and its brand. You could advise tech companies, creators and platforms on who owns what, and protect it when it is copied.
The move keeps your IP training at the centre. It widens the work from registering marks to drafting and enforcing the rights that decide how a tech business earns.
alternatives_title: What IP lawyers usually try first

alternatives.why: More files bring more of the same work. It grows the volume, not the kind of career you have.

alternatives.t: Learning to code to understand software
alternatives.why: It takes months and is not what tech companies pay a lawyer for. They need someone who reads the licence, not the code.
It deepens doctrine you already know. It rarely shows you a software licence, a content clause or a takedown in practice.

reframe_title: Software is IP. You already speak half the language.
reframe: Ownership, licensing, assignment and infringement are the core of most tech deals. Most lawyers entering tech law have to learn these from scratch. You start with them.

So the gap is not knowledge or effort. It is that tech founders do not yet see a trademark lawyer as their tech lawyer. A few tech documents with your name on them change how you are seen. Once a founder has seen you draft the IP clauses of a software contract, you are no longer only the person who files their mark.
cost: Your trademark practice can carry on comfortably. The quiet cost is that the most interesting IP questions of the next few years, about code, content and platforms, get answered by other lawyers while you renew marks.
role_h2: What tech law work looks like for an IP and trademark lawyer
role: In a software development agreement, the clause that matters most to the client is IP assignment and handover. You make sure the code passes fully to the client, and you know the difference between source code and object code, which decides what is actually handed over.

With creators and brands, you draft influencer agreements, where the IP licence and content ownership clauses decide who can reuse a video and for how long. Platforms need terms that set out IP ownership for everything users upload.

On the dispute side, tech companies need takedown notices for copied content, action against trademark abuse on marketplaces, and cybersquatting complaints. Each builds directly on enforcement work you already do. The difference is that the client is a tech business with a steady flow of content, code and sellers to protect, so the work tends to repeat.
first_artifact: On Day 3 we draft an influencer agreement with you in 5 clauses: engagement and fee, deliverables, IP licence, content ownership and brand guidelines. Two of those five are IP clauses you could draft better than most. You leave with a document that shows a creator or a brand you handle IP in the tech economy.
longer_term: The plan is about 2 hours a day: 1 hour on a new skill, 1 hour on outreach and track record. IP and takedowns sit in the plan's skills list. Over 6 months an IP lawyer could build tech IP drafts, publish short notes on platform IP issues, and approach startups and creators with work to show.

faq.q: I only know trademarks. Can I really start in tech law with that?
faq.a: It is a strong start. The script says you can learn 2 or 3 kinds of tech law work and get started, and IP ownership appears in contracts, terms and disputes.

faq.q: Will the camp go deep into software patents?
faq.a: No. The camp covers tech contracts, terms reviews, policies and the business models behind them. Its IP angle is ownership and licensing in those documents.

faq.q: Will I need an engineering or science degree?
faq.a: No. The legal work follows how the business makes money, not how the software is built.
